extracted.intended_audience: general readers of literary essays / writers interested in book-making and romantic narrative
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative principles and writing guidance embedded in Washington Irving's essays on book-making, love, and poetic creation; focuses on what makes literary works authentic, effective, or culpably derivative. Useful for authors, critics, and students of 19th-century literary practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'line upon line' compilation / literary patchwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not construct a work by stitching together morsels from many sources: “line upon line, precept upon precept, here a little and there a little.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irving criticizes the compiler who ‘takes a morsel out of one, a morsel out of another,’ producing a heterogeneous medley (the ‘witches’ cauldron’). The dream-vision of authors arrayed piecemeal in borrowed garments is an anti-pattern: such patchwork writing appears artificial, renders the author ludicrous, and invites the charge of mere pilfering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imbibe the spirit and principles of predecessors, don't appropriate their garments
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer absorbing the ‘principles of taste’ and the ‘air and spirit’ of older writers rather than copying surface features or dressing entirely in their borrowings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irving distinguishes between authors who take a few gems to augment their own voice and those who clothe themselves top-to-toe in borrowed material. The good practice is to learn tone, taste, and spirit from models while retaining one’s own shape and originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of producing ponderous erudition that will not be read
rubrics_metrics.description: Works written chiefly to advertise learning—‘some work of profound erudition, that would be purchased by every man who wished to be thought learned, placed upon a conspicuous shelf… but never read’—are a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irving caricatures the ‘lean, bilious-looking wight’ who mines worm-eaten volumes to produce unreadable tomes. The implicit criterion: scholarship should serve intelligibility and use, not merely signal erudition; write for readers, not only for reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that selective reuse can preserve and transmit beauties
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriating fine thoughts from older, obscure works can revive and perpetuate them: the author’s pilfering may serve to transmit ‘beauties and fine thoughts’ to new times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irving offers a positive framing—comparing literary re-use to seeds dispersed by birds—arguing that transformation and reappearance of ideas in new forms (history → romance, treatise → essays) can be providential and valuable when done creatively rather than slavishly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let solitude and adversity fuel imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: When the real world is shut out, the imagination can ‘create a world for itself’—solitude/adversity often provokes poetic invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tasso in his cell, and King James composing The King’s Quair while captive. Irving presents confinement as a condition that can intensify fantasy and literary productivity, a positive creative circumstance to be harnessed by writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write from personal feeling and local circumstance for greater value
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that are transcripts of genuine feeling and that contain personal/local particulars possess a ‘peculiar value’ and charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irving praises James’s Quair for breathing his immediate thoughts and for parts ‘connected with the apartment in the Tower’—this personal/local detail makes the poem present and circumstantial, increasing its appeal and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose texts suited to consolation and meditation in adversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Select source or companion texts that are appropriate for reflection under hardship—e.g., Boetius’ Consolations of Philosophy is an ‘admirable text-book for meditation under adversity.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irving recommends such works as talismans for the unfortunate: they supply maxims of morality and trains of reasoning helpful in bearing life’s ills. This is a prescriptive criterion for reading (and for the influences a writer might cultivate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional veracity in love stories: believe in broken hearts
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat romantic suffering as real and serious: ‘I believe in broken hearts, and the possibility of dying of disappointed love!’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irving argues against laughing off love-stories as mere fiction; he provides examples (the Irish patriot’s beloved) demonstrating that disappointed love can cause profound, lasting harm. For writers, the guidance is to portray love’s consequences with seriousness and psychological realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray female interiority as centered on the affections and susceptible to quiet despair
rubrics_metrics.description: A woman’s life is ‘a history of the affections’—her heart is her world, making her more fixed, secluded, and meditative; when love fails she buries it and broods in silence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irving recommends (implicitly) representing female inner life with sensitivity: show how emotional investment structures actions, social behavior, and withdrawal; avoid superficial or flippant depictions of women’s grief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict the physical consequences of prolonged melancholy realistically
rubrics_metrics.description: Disappointed love and inward sorrow often precipitate physical decline: ‘Her rest is broken… “dry sorrow drinks her blood,” until her enfeebled frame sinks under the slightest external injury.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irving links psychological wound to bodily disease (consumption, debility). As a storytelling criterion, depict the gradual, plausible deterioration of health resulting from sustained mental anguish rather than instantaneous melodrama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrast—public gaiety vs. private misery—to create poignancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing a deeply sorrowful character amid scenes of levity (e.g., a masquerade) intensifies pathos and reveals inner wretchedness: the heroine wanders like a spectre in a gay scene and draws tears when she sings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irving’s masquerade anecdote demonstrates an effective technique: juxtaposing external festivity with internal desolation (and using simple acts—e.g., a plaintive song—to expose the gulf) to move readers and spectators.
